An example list is made the complete set. Part b of the statement gives three kinds of relationship between words in a parenthesis that opens with the mark for examples. The Summary's third sentence gives the same three in a parenthesis with nothing that says they are examples, so it reads as the full list of relationships meant; every other example in this Summary and in the lane's other Summaries is marked ("for example", "such as", "as with"). The same sentence also speaks of "two words" and "both words" where the statement gives no number of words. The record's own Limits has it right (it calls the three "examples"). Fix: mark the three relationships as examples in the Summary and drop the number two. Not a near copy. Everything else holds: wording and code equal the PDF (stem and parts a to c, nothing else in the cell, no boldface, the flag false is right; example words in italics are form); the rest of the Summary and the Design notes are faithful.

Read on the page image: number 5 in the grade 6 column of the Language table, page 79: the opening line and parts a to c in order, nothing else in the cell, no boldface; the example words in italics are form. The round 1 fault is gone: the Summary now marks the three word relationships as examples and puts no number on the words. Every example in the Summary is marked as one (the figure of speech, the three relationships, the five words). "Explains what a figure of speech means" stands for the statement's verb of interpreting, whose plain sense that is. Not a near copy. Limits gives the one figure of speech and the three relationships as examples, as the cell does. For a designer, not a fault: Limits says figures of speech are "read where they occur in a text"; the statement asks only that they be taken where they occur and names no mode or medium, so a figure of speech that is heard is not excluded by it.

A general term is narrowed. The statement's second half names two general things a word or phrase can be important to, with no object and no mode: taking language in, and putting it out. The Summary gives the first as "understanding a text", which limits it to something read (in the Language strand it covers listening as well), and the second as "saying something well", which can be read as speech only and adds "well". Fix: name the two things without an object, for example understanding and expressing oneself. The first half of the Summary (both kinds of vocabulary, suited to the grade, learned and used accurately) is faithful, and it is not a near copy. Everything else holds: wording and code equal the PDF; one sentence, nothing else in the cell, no boldface. The same words stand in the grade 7 and grade 8 columns of the row (offsets 173 and 260); the script's place is the grade 6 cell.

Round 2. Wording and code hold: number 2 in the grade 6 column of the literature table, page 53, read on the page image: one sentence in two halves, nothing else in the cell, no boldface; the PDF breaks one ordinary word of the second half at a line end with a printed hyphen and the record holds it whole (form; the script's match is tolerant for that reason). The Summary's first sentence is not faithful: a verb is changed. The statement has one verb of working out, and it governs two things: the theme or central idea itself, and the way the details carry it. The Summary makes the second an explanation ("explains how"), which is another act: a student who has worked out which details carry the theme, and how, has met the statement without explaining anything, and the same table uses the verb of explaining as a demand of its own (number 6 in the same column). For a designer the difference is real: working out can be shown by choosing or marking, as the record's own "In a child's hands" has it; explaining cannot. The verb stood in the Summary before the recast too. The recast adds to it by moving the finding of the theme into a relative clause in the past ("that the student has identified"), so that the only thing the sentence asks for outright is the explanation. Fix: let the student work out both: the theme or the central idea, and how the details carry it. The rest holds: either of the two will do, as Limits says; the second sentence (a summary kept free of the student's own opinions and judgments) is faithful; the content is otherwise complete, nothing else is added, and the recast is not a near copy. Design notes are in order; RL.6.10, cited in Limits, names the three kinds of literature as said.
